Impartial

/im-PAR-shul/ — stress on PAR · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Someone who is impartial does not favor one side over another, instead making judgments based only on the facts.

A coin flip is the most impartial way to pick who goes first.

Worked Example

The referee ignored the home crowd's jeers and made an impartial call based solely on what she saw on the field.

Im (not) + partial (favoring one side). The referee does not take sides; she judges only what happened, ignoring the crowd's allegiance. This is the morpheme meaning at work: impartial = not taking sides.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

neutral: Neutral means refusing to take either side at all — a neutral country sits the war out, and a neutral observer will not even offer a verdict. Impartial steps into the contest: an impartial judge hears both sides and must decide, yet favors neither. Neutrality avoids judging; the impartial person judges fairly.

evenhanded: Evenhanded means treating all sides exactly alike — equal time, equal chances, the same rules for everyone. Impartial is about the judgment underneath: deciding on the facts without favoring anyone. A debate moderator can be evenhanded with the clock and still not impartial about who she hopes will win.

disinterested: Disinterested means having no personal stake in the outcome — nothing to gain or lose whichever way it ends. Impartial describes the judging itself: not letting favor tilt the decision. A referee betting on the match is not disinterested, however impartial his calls look; and disinterested never means bored.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

biased: unfairly favoring one side

partial: inclined toward one side — hiding inside the word itself

Where it sits · how completely favoritism is set aside — open-minded → fair → unbiased → impartial

open-minded vs. impartial: An open-minded listener is willing to hear both sides, but an impartial judge favors neither side in the final ruling.

fair vs. impartial: A fair teacher tries to treat everyone reasonably; an impartial umpire sets aside every personal preference completely.

unbiased vs. impartial: An unbiased reporter avoids leaning one way, while an impartial arbiter guarantees that neither party gets any edge at all.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — im-

Prefix — im-: not (the form in- takes before b, m, or p) (Latin)

Root — partial

Root — partial: favoring one part or side (from Latin pars, partis, 'part') (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Im- (not) + partial (favoring one part or side) = not taking sides. This word carries its own antonym inside itself: strip off the prefix and partial is exactly what an impartial judge must never be.

Use the root in a new word: participate

Use the root in a new word: participate: Everyone who wanted to participate in the science fair had to take part by Friday.

Word Choice

formal

Reach for impartial when someone is making a judgment or decision with no bias toward any side. The word emphasizes fairness based on facts alone, not personal preference or allegiance. It is the gold standard in legal, judicial, and academic contexts.
